Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations
A Separation at 1−1/e1-1/e and a 0.67670.6767 Guarantee for I.I.D. Weights

Hossein Esfandiari    MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
Abstract

The matroid prophet-secretary problem asks an online algorithm to select an independent set of elements whose nonnegative values are drawn independently and revealed in uniformly random order. Its combinatorial-auction counterpart asks the algorithm to allocate disjoint bundles to arriving buyers with independently drawn XOS valuation functions. In both problems the distributions are known, and the benchmark is the expected offline optimum. Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-competitive algorithms for both settings. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits.

For every matroid, we give a randomized (1−1/e+ε0)(1-1/e+\varepsilon_{0})-competitive algorithm, where ε0=10−6\varepsilon_{0}=10^{-6}. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes O⁡(N4)O(N^{4}) such queries in expectation and O⁡(N4​log⁡(N+2))O(N^{4}\log(N+2)) in the worst case, where NN is the number of elements.

We further consider the i.i.d. version of this problem and provide a 0.67670.6767 competitive ratio for every matroid with i.i.d. nonnegative weights from a known distribution. This guarantee even holds in fixed arrival order (a.k.a. i.i.d. matriod prophet inequalities), even when the algorithm learns the order only as the elements arrive.

Both matroid proofs measure the cost of acceptance by the rank lost among unseen elements above a given weight level. With a common law, these elements form an independent sample at a common rate. The probability that this sample spans the current element determines a quantile cutoff that pays for the loss at every level. We determine the best constant attainable by this one-step comparison. For different laws, we use a rescaled reference distribution and exploit overlap between independent optimal bases. Both matroid guarantees admit polynomial-time implementations for explicitly given finite rational distributions.

For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that 1−1/e1-1/e is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than 1−1/e1-1/e, even when the buyers’ valuations are i.i.d., every additive clause has coefficients in {0,1}\{0,1\}, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.

1 Introduction

Optimal stopping theory has long informed the design of online auctions. Hajiaghayi, Kleinberg, and Parkes [HKP04] initiated the connection between secretary problems and online auction design, and Hajiaghayi, Kleinberg, and Sandholm [HKS07] introduced prophet inequalities as a tool for designing and analyzing online auction mechanisms.11 1 These two papers were jointly recognized by the 2026 ACM SIGecom Test of Time Award [Koh26] for their contributions connecting optimal stopping with online auction and pricing mechanisms. These connections led to a broad study of how distributional information and random arrival can improve online allocation.

In a prophet inequality problem, the values are drawn independently from known distributions, and an online algorithm makes irrevocable decisions as they are revealed. Its performance is compared with a prophet who sees all realizations before choosing an optimal feasible solution. The arrival order may be adversarial. In a secretary problem, the values are fixed and unknown, but the arrival order is uniformly random. The prophet-secretary model [EHLM15] combines the distributional information of prophet inequalities with the random arrival order of secretary problems. The distributions are known in advance, and the arrival order is uniform and independent of the realized values.

The central difficulty is to use this information while preserving feasibility for future arrivals. Accepting a valuable element may prevent the selection of later elements, and allocating an item to one buyer makes it unavailable to every later buyer. Distributional information allows an algorithm to estimate these opportunity costs; random arrival also limits how often an early decision can block a more valuable later one. We study how the interaction between these two sources of information depends on the feasibility structure. Our two settings are matroid selection and combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, defined next.

1.1 Models and results

Matroid selection.

The algorithm knows a matroid M=(E,ℐ)M=(E,\mathcal{I}) on NN labeled elements and the distributions of their independent nonnegative weights XeX_{e}. On seeing a label and its weight, it irrevocably accepts or rejects the element. The accepted set must remain independent. In prophet secretary the arrival order is a uniform permutation independent of the weights. We will also consider an arbitrary order fixed independently of the weights and of the algorithm’s random bits. The benchmark in both models is

F0=𝔼​OPT⁡(M,X),OPT⁡(M,x)=max⁡∑e∈II∈ℐ⁡xe.F_{0}=\mathbb{E}\,\operatorname{OPT}(M,X),\qquad\operatorname{OPT}(M,x)=\max_{I\in\mathcal{I}}\sum_{e\in I}x_{e}.

Write ALG\operatorname{ALG} for the realized online reward. A ratio cc means 𝔼⁡[ALG]≥c​F0\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]\geq cF_{0}. For our computational bounds the algorithm may query an independence oracle on any subset of the known ground set.

Theorem 1 (Independent weights in random order).

For every finite matroid and independent nonnegative weights with F0<∞F_{0}<\infty, there is a randomized prophet-secretary algorithm with

𝔼⁡[ALG]≥(1−1/e+ε0)​F0,ε0=1.14⋅10−6.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]\geq(1-1/e+\varepsilon_{0})F_{0},\qquad\varepsilon_{0}=1.14\cdot 10^{-6}.

For explicitly given finite rational distributions, it uses O⁡(N4)O(N^{4}) independence queries in expectation and O⁡(N4​log⁡(N+2))O(N^{4}\log(N+2)) in the worst case. Its arithmetic work and number of random bits are polynomial in the input length on every execution.

When the weights share a law, the next theorem gives a larger guarantee under a weaker assumption on the order.

Theorem 2 (I.i.d. weights in a fixed order).

Let the weights of a known finite matroid be independent draws from a common known nonnegative distribution of finite mean. There is a randomized online algorithm that, in every fixed arrival order, obtains

𝔼⁡[ALG]≥c0​F0,c0=11+η0=0.6767410571​…,η02=e−1−η0,η0>0.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]\geq c_{0}F_{0},\qquad c_{0}=\frac{1}{1+\eta_{0}}=0.6767410571\ldots,\qquad\eta_{0}^{2}=e^{-1-\eta_{0}},\quad\eta_{0}>0.

The algorithm need not know the order in advance.

Averaging over a uniform permutation gives the same ratio for prophet secretary. The theorem also covers a matroid in which some labels have many substitutes and others have none. Its proof uses symmetry of the weights alone. The algorithm can be implemented by sampling and making O⁡(N4​log⁡(2​N))O(N^{4}\log(2N)) independence queries. In a real-arithmetic model it only needs evaluations of the common distribution function and its left limits at the observed weights. For a finite rational law the same ratio holds with a worst-case polynomial bound on bit complexity (Appendix A).

Welfare with XOS buyers.

There is a fixed set UU of items. Each buyer ii has a valuation drawn independently from a known distribution. When buyer ii arrives, the algorithm observes her valuation viv_{i} and assigns her a bundle SiS_{i} of unallocated items. Her valuation is XOS if it is the maximum of nonnegative additive clauses, that is, vi​(S)=max⁡∑j∈Sℓ⁡wi​ℓ​jv_{i}(S)=\max_{\ell}\sum_{j\in S}w_{i\ell j} for wi​ℓ​j≥0w_{i\ell j}\geq 0. The benchmark OPT\operatorname{OPT} is the maximum welfare ∑ivi​(Si)\sum_{i}v_{i}(S_{i}) over pairwise disjoint bundles for the realized valuations.

Theorem 3 (Sharpness for XOS welfare).

For every ξ>0\xi>0 there is a finite instance with i.i.d. buyers for which every randomized online algorithm satisfies

𝔼⁡[ALG]<(1−1/e+ξ)​𝔼​[OPT].\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]<(1-1/e+\xi)\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}].

All additive clauses have coefficients in {0,1}\{0,1\}. The bound holds with public menus of clauses and unlimited computation, even if the order of buyer identities is announced in advance.

Together with the algorithm of Ehsani et al. [EHKS18], this identifies the optimal guarantee for XOS welfare. The upper bound also follows from the i.i.d. coverage-welfare construction of Udwani and Wajc [UW26] by interchanging the roles of items and buyers. Section 9 gives the reduction and a direct proof.

Relation to the earlier version.

Theorem 1 of the first arXiv version provides a similar competitive ratio with ε0=1.01⋅10−6\varepsilon_{0}=1.01\cdot 10^{-6} for matroid prophet secretary with the same oracle complexity. The main addition here is Theorem 2 for i.i.d. distributions, with an improved competitive ratio. The previous version also established the XOS upper bound. In addition to that, here, we show that the XOS upper bound with additive tolerance ξ\xi can be witnessed on O⁡(ξ−4​log⁡(1/ξ))O(\xi^{-4}\log(1/\xi)) items (Corollary 26).

1.2 Approach and techniques

The common accounting identity.

For a nonnegative weight vector xx, put St={e:xe>t}S_{t}=\{e:x_{e}>t\} and let r⁡(S)r(S) denote the rank of SS. A maximum-weight basis found by greedy contains exactly r⁡(St)r(S_{t}) elements of StS_{t} at every height tt. Consequently,

OPT⁡(M,x)=∫0∞r⁡(St)​𝑑t.\operatorname{OPT}(M,x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}r(S_{t})\,dt. (1.1)

To see what one online decision costs at a given height, fix the arriving nonloop ee, and let AA consist of the unseen elements above that height. If AA spans ee, taking ee consumes one unit of the rank available to AA. If AA does not span ee, taking ee costs AA nothing, but passing over ee can lose a unit of rank when its own weight exceeds tt. Both matroid algorithms price these two possibilities. The common-law assumption changes what can be learned from a single sampling experiment.

One quantile cutoff for every height.

Suppose the common upper-tail probability at height tt is vv. In the residual matroid, the unseen elements above tt form a set obtained by retaining each unseen element independently with probability vv. Write Se​(v)S_{e}(v) for the probability that this set fails to span ee. An upper quantile qq specifies a threshold. The rule takes ee on the best qq fraction of its draws, breaking ties at atoms by an independent random choice. At any height with tail probability vv this rule earns min⁡{q,v}\min\{q,v\} in expected count. Its expected cost to the remaining rank is

v​Se​(v)+q⁡(1−Se​(v)).vS_{e}(v)+q(1-S_{e}(v)).

The first term is the expected cost of deletion. The second is the extra cost of contracting ee when the rule accepts. In particular, the decision pays for itself exactly at v=qv=q.

The same cutoff must also pay for the narrow bands v<qv<q and the wide bands v>qv>q. For v<qv<q there is a loss only when the unseen sample spans ee. For v>qv>q there is a loss only when it fails to do so. This is where the shape of SeS_{e} matters. Calibrate qq by Se​(q)=e−aS_{e}(q)=e^{-a}. A product-measure inequality bounds Se​(v)S_{e}(v) from below by e−av/qe^{-av/q} for v<qv<q and from above by the same curve for v>qv>q. Thus the excess cost per unit of reward is at most aa on narrow bands and at most maxx≥1⁡(x−1)​e−a​x=e−1−a/a\max_{x\geq 1}(x-1)e^{-ax}=e^{-1-a}/a on wide bands. Equating the two gives exactly a=η0a=\eta_{0} in Theorem 2. The bound holds after fixing both the history and the next label, which explains why this proof needs no randomness in the arrival order. A sequence of parallel elements makes the one-step comparison sharp. The optimal rank-one policy can do better by compensating for a loss at one step with a gain at another.

Beyond the one-step comparison.

For i.i.d. weights in random order, the distinction between a local guarantee and the optimal ratio can be made precise. Follow an arbitrary policy through its sequence of residual matroids. If it accepts a label with conditional probability qq in a given minor, replacing that decision by a top-qq cutoff sends the same probability mass to each child and earns at least as much in every upper band. Thus a policy can be described by a flow on labeled minors. In fact a single flow attains the worst-law ratio of the matroid simultaneously for all common laws. If some finite set of band targets were incompatible, a separating hyperplane would supply nonnegative weights for the bands. Those weights are the increments of a finite-support common law on which every policy misses its target. Appendix B proves this characterization and a companion identity that compares the optimal online price with the prophet’s realized replacement cost on the same random restriction.

Pricing a decision when the laws differ.

With arbitrary marginals, the unseen set at height tt samples different labels at different rates. There is no common quantile at which to apply the preceding comparison. We work directly with the weighted optimum and use the randomness of the next label. For a nonloop ee, fix the other weights and let τe\tau_{e} be the difference between their optima after deleting and contracting ee. Deleting ee from the original instance loses (Xe−τe)+(X_{e}-\tau_{e})^{+}, where u+=max⁡{u,0}u^{+}=\max\{u,0\}. The sum of these losses in expectation, divided by the number of remaining labels, is the cost of rejecting the next arrival.

A large expected deletion loss can arise in two ways. An element might rarely draw a very large weight, or it might regularly beat its replacement by a substantial margin. To distinguish them, draw its weight a second time, keeping the other weights fixed. The quantity (min⁡{Xe,Xe′}−τe)+(\min\{X_{e},X^{\prime}_{e}\}-\tau_{e})^{+} counts the part of the surplus that survives the second draw. Summing its expectation over labels gives the stable surplus. Roughly speaking, rare high offers favor a posted price, whereas persistent membership in an optimum favors a basis-exchange rule. To make this distinction quantitative, we first choose the distribution against which to measure the two surpluses.

Starting from the actual upper tails, multiply every tail probability by a common scale factor qq near one, capping the result at one. Let FqF_{q} be the expected optimum of this reference instance. The potential is (1−θ​q)​Fq(1-\theta q)F_{q}, with θ\theta slightly below 1/e1/e. Increasing qq makes the reference optimum larger and its coefficient smaller. The rate at which FqF_{q} grows is closely related to deletion surplus. At a given height, increasing one label’s probability changes expected rank precisely when the other active labels fail to span it. Integrating over heights relates the derivative of FqF_{q} to the sum of the deletion losses. The stable surplus bounds the contribution of tails that reach the cap. Concavity then allows the algorithm to choose qq without sacrificing the potential inherited from earlier decisions.

Small stable surplus. The algorithm posts a price proportional to the expected difference between deleting and contracting the next label. Charging the price only to elements of the optimal basis loses too much. An element outside that basis can still clear its price, and a rule processing one arrival can collect its surplus. To quantify this contribution we cap the reference weights at scaled contraction prices and apply a tangent inequality for the expected rank under Poisson rounding [DRY11]. After integrating over heights, the extra surplus covers the expected deletion loss. The rule processes one arrival and repeats in the resulting minor.

Large stable surplus. Two independent reference optima then have substantial overlap. To measure the relevant overlap, count a shared element at height tt only when it belongs to both optima and both its weights exceed tt. Integrating this expected count gives a weighted overlap QQ. Section 4.2 lower-bounds QQ by comparing greedy and reverse-greedy bases of each level set. The algorithm can spend this overlap in the last part of the arrival sequence. It maintains virtual bases containing all previously accepted labels, updating each basis by an injective exchange whenever a new label is accepted. Early on it randomly thins acceptances to control the rate at which an exchange can displace any particular element. In a short final interval it removes this thinning. The corresponding loss in the baseline guarantee is quadratic in the length of that interval, whereas the gain from overlap is linear. Near the endpoints of the reference search, the baseline continuation has enough slack to pay for the final interval even at zero overlap. These comparisons cover all branches of the algorithm.

Why the XOS upper bound survives identical distributions.

The auction construction has a public collection of partitions of the items, with one partition for every possible set of distinct buyer types. If the nn realized types are distinct, the prophet can choose their common partition and give each buyer a different part, attaining full welfare. An online allocation fixes a supporting clause for each bundle as soon as it is assigned. Each such clause points to a partition indexed by just nn types, so with a sufficiently large type space a later buyer is unlikely to be able to use the same partition. The construction makes one part from each of nn distinct partitions cover exactly a 1−(1−1/n)n1-(1-1/n)^{n} fraction of the items. This counting identity limits the total welfare even when all valuation types and their probabilities are public.

1.3 Related work

Independent distributions and random arrival.

The classical prophet inequality compares an online stopping rule with the expected maximum of independent nonnegative random variables [KS77]. Its connections to online auctions and pricing were developed in [HKP04, HKS07].22 2 These two papers received the 2026 ACM SIGecom Test of Time Award [Koh26]. Esfandiari et al. [EHLM15] introduced the prophet-secretary model. In an arbitrary fixed order, the matroid inequality of Kleinberg and Weinberg [KW12] and the posted-price mechanism of Feldman, Gravin, and Lucier [FGL15] give a factor of 1/21/2 for matroid selection and XOS welfare, respectively. Ehsani et al. [EHKS18] showed that random arrival raises both guarantees to 1−1/e1-1/e. For a single choice, Azar, Chiplunkar, and Kaplan [ACK18] broke this barrier, followed by Correa, Saona, and Ziliotto [CSZ21]. Chen et al. [CHLT25] obtained 0.6880.688 for a single choice and 0.6410.641 for prophet-secretary matching.

Identical distributions.

In rank one the sharp constant over all horizons is 0.745440​…0.745440\ldots. Hill and Kertz [HK82] obtained the sharp finite-horizon constants, and Kertz [Ker86] determined their limit. Abolhassani et al. [AEE+17] gave a threshold rule attaining 0.7380.738 asymptotically. Correa et al. [CFH+21] matched the limiting upper bound with a guarantee for every horizon. For kk choices, Brustle, Perez-Salazar, and Verdugo [BPSV26] characterized the finite-horizon i.i.d. ratio by a linear program. A cardinality constraint is invariant under relabeling. On a general matroid, exchanging two labels can change feasibility even when their weights have the same law. In the related random-assignment secretary problem [Sot13], an unknown list of weights is assigned uniformly to the labels. Conditioning i.i.d. weights on their unordered multiset gives this assignment. Our algorithm also uses the common law to compute weight quantiles.

Contention resolution and basis exchange.

An online contention-resolution scheme selects a feasible subset from a random set of active elements [FSZ16]. Lee and Singla [LS18] obtained the tight factor 1−1/e1-1/e for matroids under random arrival against the ex-ante relaxation. The distinction between benchmarks already matters in rank one. If each of nn elements independently has value one with probability 1/n1/n and zero otherwise, the ex-ante value is one, whereas the expected optimum is 1−(1−1/n)n1-(1-1/n)^{n}. Our matroid guarantees use the latter benchmark. Adamczyk and Włodarczyk [AW18] used basis-exchange maps of the kind proved by Brualdi [Bru69] to maintain feasible sets under random arrivals. Our heterogeneous algorithm applies exchanges to bases drawn from a reference distribution and uses the overlap of two such optima to bound the gain over 1−1/e1-1/e. The rank inequality in its analysis uses the concavity of Poisson-rounded matroid rank [DRY11].

Information about weights.

In the matroid secretary problem [BIK07], the weights are fixed and unknown. Recent algorithms give a constant guarantee in this model [Sin26, Hua26, ABH+26]. The single-sample prophet model gives one independent sample from each law. Azar, Kleinberg, and Weinberg studied its connection to secretary algorithms [AKW14]. For a fixed arrival order independent of samples, realizations, and private randomness, Abdi et al. [ABHM26, ABH+26] obtained the sharp factor 1/21/2 on every matroid. Our algorithms use known distributions.

Online welfare.

In the item-arrival model with coverage valuations, Kapralov, Post, and Vondrák [KPV13] proved that greedy achieves 1−1/e1-1/e on i.i.d. arrivals and that a polynomial-time algorithm improving this factor would imply NP=RP\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}. Udwani and Wajc [UW26] proved the same upper bound for unrestricted computation even when the common distribution is known. Chawla and Dang [CD26, Appendix D] used a coverage-to-XOS transformation in the free-disposal model. Section 9.3 explains how it carries the information-theoretic bound over to irrevocable buyer-arrival allocation.

Organization.

After the common matroid preliminaries, Section 3 gives the i.i.d. algorithm and proves the sharp bound on its one-step analysis. For general marginals, Sections 4 and 5 prove the threshold and exchange bounds. Sections 6–8 use these bounds in the online algorithm. Section 9 gives the auction construction. Appendices A and B treat implementation and optimal policies for i.i.d. weights. Appendices C and D give the bit complexity and the numerical certificate for general marginals.

2 Matroid preliminaries

Matroids and residual instances.

We use the matroid and prophet-secretary models of Section 1.1. For M=(E,ℐ)M=(E,\mathcal{I}), the rank of S⊆ES\subseteq E is

rM(S)=max{|I|:I⊆S,I∈ℐ}.r_{M}(S)=\max\{|I|:I\subseteq S,\ I\in\mathcal{I}\}.

A basis is a maximal independent set. Write ℬ⁡(M)\mathcal{B}(M) for the set of bases, all of size rM​(E)r_{M}(E). The closure of SS is clM⁡(S)={e∈E:rM​(S∪{e})=rM​(S)}\operatorname{cl}_{M}(S)=\{e\in E:r_{M}(S\cup\{e\})=r_{M}(S)\}. We say SS spans ee if e∈clM⁡(S)e\in\operatorname{cl}_{M}(S) and spans TT if T⊆clM⁡(S)T\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_{M}(S). A flat is a set equal to its closure. An element is a loop if its singleton is dependent and a coloop if it belongs to every basis. Two distinct nonloops are parallel if their pair has rank one. Subscripts are omitted when the matroid is clear.

The restriction to R⊆ER\subseteq E is M|R=(R,{I∈ℐ:I⊆R})M|_{R}=(R,\{I\in\mathcal{I}:I\subseteq R\}), and the deletion of RR is M∖R=M|E∖RM\setminus R=M|_{E\setminus R}. The contraction M/RM/R has ground set E∖RE\setminus R and rank function

rM/R​(S)=rM​(S∪R)−rM​(R).r_{M/R}(S)=r_{M}(S\cup R)-r_{M}(R).

This definition also applies when RR is dependent. If RR is independent, SS is independent in M/RM/R exactly when S∪RS\cup R is independent in MM. For a single element, write M∖eM\setminus e and M/eM/e. A matroid obtained by deletions and contractions is a minor. A set JJ disjoint from TT is independent over TT if rM​(T∪J)=rM​(T)+|J|r_{M}(T\cup J)=r_{M}(T)+|J|.

A circuit is an inclusionwise minimal dependent set. If BB is a basis and e∉Be\notin B, the unique circuit in B∪{e}B\cup\{e\} is the fundamental circuit of ee with respect to BB. We use the shorthand B−f+e=(B∖{f})∪{e}B-f+e=(B\setminus\{f\})\cup\{e\}.

At a residual state, the accepted independent set is contracted and rejected elements are deleted. We discard loops. Independence of the weights allows us to use the original distribution on each surviving label. To implement a matroid independence query in the residual minor, adjoin the already contracted independent set and make one query to the original matroid independence oracle.

Weighted bases.

We fix a total order of the labels throughout. The greedy algorithm scans elements in decreasing order of weight, using this label order to break ties, and adds an element whenever independence is preserved. It chooses a canonical maximum-weight basis, denoted B⁡(y)B(y). Zero-weight elements are used to complete the basis. A product distribution is a joint distribution with mutually independent coordinates. For a value vector YY with a product distribution, write F⁡(M,Y)=𝔼​OPT⁡(M,Y)F(M,Y)=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{OPT}(M,Y), omitting the matroid and distribution when fixed. The distributions may have atoms, including an atom at zero. We write u+=max⁡{u,0}u^{+}=\max\{u,0\}, use 𝟏​{A}\mathbf{1}\{A\} for the indicator of an event AA, and put [k]={1,…,k}[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}.

3 Identically distributed weights

Suppose that the weights are independent draws from a common distribution FF on [0,∞)[0,\infty) of finite mean. Fix an arrival order independently of the draws and the algorithm’s randomness. We now prove Theorem 2. At each step NN denotes the minor on the remaining labels, obtained by contracting accepted elements and deleting rejected elements. We write PN​(F)P_{N}(F) for its expected offline optimum.

Randomly break ties within each atom of FF. More precisely, when ee has weight xx, draw its upper quantile UeU_{e} uniformly from [1−F⁡(x),1−F⁡(x−)][1-F(x),1-F(x-)]. These quantiles are independent and uniform on [0,1][0,1], with the smallest quantiles corresponding to the largest weights. For 0≤v≤10\leq v\leq 1, let BvB_{v} be the elements with quantiles at most vv. Equivalently, sample each label independently with probability vv. Define

RN​(v)=𝔼​rN​(Bv),SeN​(v)=Pr⁡(e∉clN⁡(Bv∖{e})).R_{N}(v)=\mathbb{E}r_{N}(B_{v}),\qquad S_{e}^{N}(v)=\Pr\bigl(e\notin\operatorname{cl}_{N}(B_{v}\setminus\{e\})\bigr).

Here BvB_{v} is sampled on E⁡(N)E(N), and rNr_{N} is the rank function of NN. The function SeNS_{e}^{N} measures how hard it is to replace ee at a given weight level. In particular, it depends on the unseen labels, but has no dependence on their order.

The rule.

Fix a parameter a>0a>0. Reject loops and accept coloops. For any other arrival ee, accept if SeN​(Ue)≥e−aS_{e}^{N}(U_{e})\geq e^{-a}. Equivalently, accept the best qq fraction of the draws, where qq is the solution to SeN​(q)=e−aS_{e}^{N}(q)=e^{-a}. The solution is unique since SeNS_{e}^{N} is a nonincreasing polynomial, with SeN​(0)=1S_{e}^{N}(0)=1 and SeN​(1)=0S_{e}^{N}(1)=0. Its values lie strictly between 00 and 11 in the interior. The sampled implementation in Appendix A needs only independence queries.

Theorem 4 (One cutoff for all weight levels).

For every v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1], the expected number of accepted labels in BvB_{v} is at least c⁡(a)​RM​(v)c(a)R_{M}(v), where

c⁡(a)=11+max⁡{a,e−1−a/a}.c(a)=\frac{1}{1+\max\{a,e^{-1-a}/a\}}.

Consequently the rule earns at least c⁡(a)​PM​(F)c(a)P_{M}(F) in every fixed order. The best choice of aa is the unique positive solution η0\eta_{0} to η02=e−1−η0\eta_{0}^{2}=e^{-1-\eta_{0}}, giving c0=(1+η0)−1=0.6767410571​…c_{0}=(1+\eta_{0})^{-1}=0.6767410571\ldots.

The proof uses one property of product measures. It controls the probability that ee increases rank at all sampling rates from its value at the cutoff.

Lemma 5.

If ee is neither a loop nor a coloop, let S⁡(v)=SeN​(v)S(v)=S_{e}^{N}(v) and τ⁡(v)=−log⁡(1−v)\tau(v)=-\log(1-v). Both −logS(v)/τ(v)-\log S(v)/\tau(v) and −logS(v)/v-\log S(v)/v are nondecreasing on (0,1)(0,1).

Corollary 6 (A threshold in the original weights).

3.1 How much can a one-step comparison prove?

The quantitative loss in Theorem 4 is sharp for the local comparison used in its proof. This statement already holds in rank one, where the optimal stopping rule attains the larger Hill–Kertz constant [CFH+21]. The example identifies where a stronger argument must use the continuation of the policy.

Proposition 7.

Suppose a rule, possibly randomized, earns at every arrival and every quantile level vv at least a fraction cc of the expected one-step drop in RN​(v)R_{N}(v), on every matroid with a common weight law. Then c≤c0c\leq c_{0}. The same upper bound holds for a rule required only to cover the one-step drop in PN​(F)P_{N}(F), even when the rule can depend on FF.

In rank one, a stopping rule attains the larger Hill–Kertz constant by balancing gains across arrivals. Whether the same 0.74544​…0.74544\ldots guarantee holds on every matroid in random order remains open. Appendix B characterizes the optimum in that model by allowing precisely this kind of compensation.

4 Reference distributions and structural inequalities

The algorithm compares product distributions obtained by multiplying every upper tail by the same factor. This section establishes the two inequalities it needs. The first converts surplus that survives a second draw into overlap between two optimum bases (Lemma 10). The second lower-bounds the surplus available to an online threshold rule when little of the deletion surplus survives (Corollary 15).

Information and computation.

The algorithm knows the ground set, the matroid through its independence oracle, and the labeled input distributions. At an arrival it observes the label and value and must decide immediately. The algorithm draws its reference samples using fresh randomness. When it constructs a candidate for the currently arriving label, it may fix that coordinate at the observed value and sample all other coordinates independently from their reference distributions.

For the computational part of Theorem 1, each distribution is an explicit finite list of rational values and probabilities; let LL be their total binary encoding length. We first analyze exact random draws. Appendix C replaces them by finite procedures and proves a worst-case polynomial bound on arithmetic operations and random bits.

Symbolic parameters.

Fix positive rational constants δ,θ,ε,η,ρ,s\delta,\theta,\varepsilon,\eta,\rho,s, with δ\delta dyadic, meaning an integer divided by a power of two. Define

J=[q−,q+]=[1−4​δ,1+4​δ],a⁡(q)=1−θ​q,d∗​(q)=1−a⁡(q)a⁡(q).J=[q_{-},q_{+}]=[1-4\delta,1+4\delta],\qquad a(q)=1-\theta q,\qquad d_{*}(q)=\frac{1-a(q)}{a(q)}. (4.1)

The potential is a⁡(q)​Fqa(q)F_{q}, where FqF_{q} is the expected reference optimum defined below. The algorithm uses η\eta to decide whether to invoke the basis-exchange continuation. Its last δ\delta units of time will play a different role from the rest. The estimates have accuracy parameter ε\varepsilon and error budget ρ\rho. The constant ss enters only in the rank inequality of Lemma 13. We use the following bounds:

0<ε<δ≤18,ε≤110,0<θ<1,0<ρ<1,s>0,η>10ε,12≤a⁡(q)≤34(q∈J),(maxq∈J⁡a⁡(q))​q+≤1,d∗​(q)−20​ε<1(q∈J).\begin{gathered}0<\varepsilon<\delta\leq\tfrac{1}{8},\qquad\varepsilon\leq\tfrac{1}{10},\qquad 0<\theta<1,\quad 0<\rho<1,\quad s>0,\quad\eta>10\varepsilon,\\ \tfrac{1}{2}\leq a(q)\leq\tfrac{3}{4}\quad(q\in J),\qquad\bigl(\max_{q\in J}a(q)\bigr)q_{+}\leq 1,\qquad d_{*}(q)-20\varepsilon<1\quad(q\in J).\end{gathered} (4.2)

The proof of Theorem 1 will use three further scalar inequalities, stated in Section 8. Their meaning will be clear after the two possible continuations have been analyzed. Appendix D gives a single choice satisfying all of them.

4.2 Stable surplus implies overlap

The derivative bounds involve HH, but the continuation earns additional reward in proportion to QQ. To relate them, run greedy twice on the same active set, once in decreasing priority order and once in reverse. An active coloop must survive both scans.

Lemma 10 (Stable surplus and overlap).

For every independent nonnegative value vector,

H2≤Q⁡(F−D+H)≤F​Q.H^{2}\leq Q(F-D+H)\leq FQ. (4.8)
Proof.

Fix a height zz and suppress it from the notation. Let SS activate the labels independently with probabilities pe=ℙ⁡(Ye>z)p_{e}=\mathbb{P}(Y_{e}>z). Independently of these activity indicators, draw for each label a latent value from its conditional law given Ye>zY_{e}>z. Labels with pe=0p_{e}=0 can be omitted. For fixed latent priorities, let ae+a_{e}^{+} be the probability that the active labels preceding ee do not span it, and let ae−a_{e}^{-} be the corresponding probability for the labels following it. These events depend on disjoint sets of independent activity indicators. Nonspan by all other active labels implies both events, so

ρe≤ae+​ae−.\rho_{e}\leq a_{e}^{+}a_{e}^{-}.

The function ae+a_{e}^{+} is nondecreasing in ee’s latent value and nonincreasing in each other latent value; ae−a_{e}^{-} has the opposite monotonicities. Product association, after reversing the order of the other coordinates, therefore gives

We next relate deletion surplus to the surplus above deterministic thresholds. The appropriate deterministic prices are expected contraction costs:

πe=𝔼​max⁡{Ye,τe}=me+de.\pi_{e}=\mathbb{E}\max\{Y_{e},\tau_{e}\}=m_{e}+d_{e}.

The choice of a fixed basis will let us integrate a rank inequality over all heights. The gap GG measures how much we lose by charging the contraction prices of this basis against the optimum.

Lemma 11 (Expected contraction prices).

One has 0≤P≤F0\leq P\leq F. Every strict superlevel set TT of π\pi is spanned by B∩TB\cap T, and B∩TB\cap T is a basis of TT. Moreover,

G=∫0∞𝔼⁡[r⁡(Sz)−|B∩cl⁡(Sz)|]​𝑑z,Sz={e:Ye>z},G=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}\bigl[r(S_{z})-|B\cap\operatorname{cl}(S_{z})|\bigr]\,dz,\qquad S_{z}=\{e:Y_{e}>z\}, (4.9)

Finally, the greedy characterization of a maximum-weight basis shows that B∩TB\cap T is a basis of every strict superlevel set TT of π\pi. ∎

Fix b∈(0,1)b\in(0,1) and cap each reference value at b​πeb\pi_{e}:

Y~e=min⁡{Ye,b​πe},Δb=b​P−𝔼​OPT⁡(M,Y~)≥0.\widetilde{Y}_{e}=\min\{Y_{e},b\pi_{e}\},\qquad\Delta_{b}=bP-\mathbb{E}\operatorname{OPT}(M,\widetilde{Y})\geq 0.

Sb\displaystyle S_{b} =∑e𝔼​(Ye−b​me)+,\displaystyle=\sum_{e}\mathbb{E}(Y_{e}-bm_{e})^{+}, Sπ,b\displaystyle S_{\pi,b} =∑e𝔼​(Ye−b​πe)+,\displaystyle=\sum_{e}\mathbb{E}(Y_{e}-b\pi_{e})^{+},

Sb≥Sπ,b≥(1−b)​F+b​G+Δb,D≤Sπ,b+Kb.S_{b}\geq S_{\pi,b}\geq(1-b)F+bG+\Delta_{b},\qquad D\leq S_{\pi,b}+K_{b}. (4.10)

To bound KbK_{b}, we use the concavity of Poisson-rounded matroid rank, which underlies the rounding method of Dughmi, Roughgarden, and Yan [DRY11]. A tangent inequality evaluated at one scaled basis vector suffices here. The parameter ss below will be chosen in Appendix D.

Lemma 13 (A fixed Poisson tangent).

Let N0N_{0} be a rank-r0r_{0} matroid with a basis C0C_{0}, and let RR activate labels independently with probabilities pep_{e}. Put

ρe=ℙ⁡(e∉clN0⁡(R∖e)),m=∑f∈C0ℙ⁡(f∉clN0⁡(R)).\rho_{e}=\mathbb{P}(e\notin\operatorname{cl}_{N_{0}}(R\setminus e)),\qquad m=\sum_{f\in C_{0}}\mathbb{P}(f\notin\operatorname{cl}_{N_{0}}(R)).

∑epe​ρe≤∑epe2​ρe+r0​e−s+s​m.\sum_{e}p_{e}\rho_{e}\leq\sum_{e}p_{e}^{2}\rho_{e}+r_{0}e^{-s}+sm. (4.11)

For distinct labels e,fe,f, the mixed second derivative is minus the probability that ee and ff are parallel nonloops in N0/RxN_{0}/R_{x}, with contracted labels treated as loops. The mixed discrete rank difference is −1-1 exactly for a parallel pair of nonloops; the factors e−xe−xfe^{-x_{e}-x_{f}} enforce the absence of e,fe,f from RxR_{x}.

Thus the negative Hessian is the expectation of a block matrix with one all-ones block for each nonloop parallel class of N0/RxN_{0}/R_{x} and zeros elsewhere. Each block is positive semidefinite, so ff is concave. At x=λx=\lambda, write ue=∂ef⁡(λ)=(1−pe)​ρeu_{e}=\partial_{e}f(\lambda)=(1-p_{e})\rho_{e}. This proves the claim. Coordinates with pe=1p_{e}=1 follow by continuity of the finite Bernoulli expectations. Rank zero is immediate. ∎

Corollary 15 (Threshold surplus).

If F>0F>0, then for every b∈(0,1)b\in(0,1) and s>0s>0,

SbF≥1−b+bb+s​(DF−(1−b)−HF−b​e−s).\frac{S_{b}}{F}\geq 1-b+\frac{b}{b+s}\left(\frac{D}{F}-(1-b)-\frac{H}{F}-be^{-s}\right). (4.14)

5 A virtual basis-exchange continuation

Suppose two independent reference optima often contain the same valuable elements. We will use this overlap late in the arrival sequence. Each accepted label is inserted into every reference basis by an exchange. The algorithm stores only one record per acceptance. It can then recover any particular basis by replaying the exchanges starting from its original greedy basis.

As in the survival simulation of [ABH+26, Section 6], the algorithm tests a survival event on an auxiliary random sample. Here a test draws a reference basis and replays the accepted records. Lemma 18 gives the resulting acceptance rates.

Fix a loopless residual matroid MM on nn labels, a parameter q∈Jq\in J, and the product reference law μ\mu of Y=YqY=Y^{q}. We first describe the algorithm for finitely supported distributions, so that its screening probabilities are ratios of point masses. The approximation argument at the end of Appendix D extends the existence guarantee to general distributions. Write DeD_{e} and DeqD_{e}^{q} for the original and reference distributions. Put

λ=1q,t0=1−δ,α=e−λ​t0,ω=α−λ​δ,\lambda=\frac{1}{q},\qquad t_{0}=1-\delta,\qquad\alpha=e^{-\lambda t_{0}},\qquad\omega=\alpha-\lambda\delta, (5.1)

and assume ω>0\omega>0. Define

Φδ(q,z)=1−α+αω(1−e−λδ/ω)(1+(1−α)z).\Phi_{\delta}(q,z)=1-\alpha+\alpha\omega(1-e^{-\lambda\delta/\omega})\bigl(1+(1-\alpha)z\bigr). (5.2)

For δ=0\delta=0, this is the familiar 1−e−1/q1-e^{-1/q} guarantee. For a short positive final interval, its dependence on zz will give the improvement.

Proposition 16 (Virtual continuation).

If F=𝔼​OPT⁡(M,Y)>0F=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{OPT}(M,Y)>0, there is a feasible online continuation with

𝔼⁡[ALG]≥Φδ​(q,Q/F)​F.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]\geq\Phi_{\delta}(q,Q/F)F.

In the exact-randomness model it uses O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) matroid independence queries in expectation. Its decisions use only the current arrival and previously accepted records.

5.1 Updating virtual bases

Fix the label order from Section 2. For each pair of bases C,BC,B, we need one injective exchange map from CC to BB. The same map must be used regardless of which source element is queried.

Lemma 17 (A canonical exchange map).

For bases C,BC,B, one can construct a bijection ϕC,B:C→B\phi_{C,B}:C\to B fixing C∩BC\cap B pointwise such that

B−ϕC,B​(f)+f∈ℬ⁡(M)(f∈C).B-\phi_{C,B}(f)+f\in\mathcal{B}(M)\qquad(f\in C).

The map uses O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) matroid independence queries.

Proof.

Keep the target basis BB fixed and initialize a working basis C′=CC^{\prime}=C. Fix every element of C∩BC\cap B. Until C′=BC^{\prime}=B, take the first f∈C′∖Bf\in C^{\prime}\setminus B in the label order and scan b∈B∖C′b\in B\setminus C^{\prime} in that order. Choose the first bb such that both B−b+fB-b+f and C′−f+bC^{\prime}-f+b are bases. Assign ϕC,B​(f)=b\phi_{C,B}(f)=b and replace C′C^{\prime} by C′−f+bC^{\prime}-f+b.

Such a bb exists. Let Γ⊆B+f\Gamma\subseteq B+f be the fundamental circuit of ff, and let H=cl⁡(C′∖f)H=\operatorname{cl}(C^{\prime}\setminus f). Since f∉Hf\notin H and f∈cl⁡(Γ∖f)f\in\operatorname{cl}(\Gamma\setminus f), some b∈Γ∖fb\in\Gamma\setminus f lies outside HH. This element belongs to B∖C′B\setminus C^{\prime} and permits both exchanges.

Each step removes one original source element outside BB and adds one previously absent element of BB. Thus the assigned images do not repeat, and the procedure ends at BB. Every image satisfies the required exchange property with respect to the unchanged target. If d=|C∖B|d=|C\setminus B|, at most 2​(d+(d−1)+⋯+1)=d⁡(d+1)2(d+(d-1)+\cdots+1)=d(d+1) queries are used. ∎

To evaluate only ϕC,B​(e)\phi_{C,B}(e), the algorithm stops this fixed scan when ee’s image is assigned. The scan order does not depend on ee. This consistency is what allows us to charge all possible insertions to distinct target elements.

Reference realizations and accepted records.

For a reference realization yy, let By0B_{y}^{0} be its canonical maximum-weight basis. The continuation algorithm stores records (ei,ti,Ci)(e_{i},t_{i},C_{i}), one for each acceptance, where CiC_{i} is the candidate basis that justified that acceptance. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the ordered list of accepted records. Define Replay⁡(y,ℋ,t)\operatorname{Replay}(y,\mathcal{H},t) by starting with B=By0B=B_{y}^{0} and replaying the accepted records with ti≤tt_{i}\leq t in order:

B←B−ϕCi,B​(ei)+ei.B\leftarrow B-\phi_{C_{i},B}(e_{i})+e_{i}.

Write By​(t)=Replay⁡(y,ℋ,t)B_{y}(t)=\operatorname{Replay}(y,\mathcal{H},t). At an arrival, evaluate this basis using the records of earlier acceptances. The continuation always samples from the same law on the same matroid MM. In particular, a fresh reference basis may contain a previously rejected label.

Every current basis contains the accepted set AtA_{t}. Indeed, the source and target bases at an insertion both contain the previous accepted set, which the exchange map fixes pointwise. A pair (e,y)(e,y) is live at tt if ye>0y_{e}>0 and e∈By​(t)∖Ate\in B_{y}(t)\setminus A_{t}. Only accepted labels are inserted, so an unaccepted label present in By​(t)B_{y}(t) also belongs to By0B_{y}^{0}. Once a live pair disappears it cannot become live again.

For a fixed accepted history, define

𝒦e,t​(d​y)\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{e,t}(dy) =𝟏​{(e,y)​ is live at ​t}​μ​(d​y),\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\{(e,y)\text{ is live at }t\}\mu(dy), (5.3)
ke​(t)\displaystyle k_{e}(t) =∫𝒦e,t​(dy),\displaystyle=\int\mathcal{K}_{e,t}(dy), we​(t)\displaystyle w_{e}(t) =∫ye​𝒦e,t​(dy).\displaystyle=\int y_{e}\,\mathcal{K}_{e,t}(dy).

These are analysis quantities. The algorithm tests liveness in sampled reference realizations and never evaluates these integrals. For every reference realization, the live labels form a subset of By0B_{y}^{0} and of By​(t)∖AtB_{y}(t)\setminus A_{t}. Consequently they are feasible in M/AtM/A_{t}, and ∑ewe​(t)≤F\sum_{e}w_{e}(t)\leq F.

5.2 The arrival rule

Assign independent uniform times in [0,1][0,1] to the residual labels. In the random-permutation model, this means drawing and sorting nn independent uniform numbers, then attaching them in order to the remaining arrivals. The rule uses the current time and accepted records; unused future clocks and rejected observations do not enter its decisions.

Candidate and probe draws are independent. A candidate uses the observed ee-coordinate, whereas each probe samples that coordinate afresh. After t0t_{0}, the algorithm accepts every screened live candidate.

The reference screen is a valid probability. The function u↦min⁡{1,q​u}u\mapsto\min\{1,qu\} is qq-Lipschitz, so each positive reference atom has mass at most qq times the corresponding original atom. Multiplying the original atom by the screen probability and sampling the other coordinates gives the candidate-realization submeasure λ​𝒦e,t\lambda\mathcal{K}_{e,t} before the Poisson test.

Every acceptance is feasible because its candidate basis contains all earlier accepted labels. Evaluating a fresh reference realization requires a greedy scan and at most nn exchange replays, hence O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) queries. There is at most one candidate realization and an expected two probe realizations per arrival, giving O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}) expected queries. It remains to prove the reward guarantee.

5.3 The law of the accepted process

A missing label may still be on its way, or it may already have been rejected. We keep both possibilities when conditioning on accepted records. To state the calculation, attach to each acceptance a mark, such as the value and the reference realization used in the decision. The history records the labels, times, and marks of acceptances. Given this history, the intensity of an acceptance with mark in a set is its conditional probability per unit time.

Lemma 18 (Acceptance intensity).

For each label ee, let TeT_{e} be a uniform arrival time, XeX_{e} its actual value, and ReR_{e} a private random tape. These triples are independent across labels, and their coordinates are independent. Suppose the decision at an arrival uses only the accepted marked history. For a frozen prefix hh, let Ψe​(h,t,Xe,Re)\Psi_{e}(h,t,X_{e},R_{e}) be either rejection or an acceptance mark, and let νe,h,t\nu_{e,h,t} be its acceptance subprobability kernel under the unconditional law of (Xe,Re)(X_{e},R_{e}).

Along a prescribed accepted path, write hth_{t} for the prefix before tt and, for a label not yet accepted, put

Se​(t)=1−∫0tνe,hu,u​(ℳ)​𝑑u,S_{e}(t)=1-\int_{0}^{t}\nu_{e,h_{u},u}(\mathcal{M})\,du,

where ℳ\mathcal{M} is the acceptance-mark space. Wherever Se>0S_{e}>0, the marked acceptance intensity, with respect to the history of accepted marks, is νe,ht,t/Se​(t)\nu_{e,h_{t},t}/S_{e}(t).

Proof.

Fix a marked accepted path through time tt. A label absent from this path satisfies precisely

{Te>t}∪{Te≤t,Ψe(hTe,Te,Xe,Re) is rejection}.\{T_{e}>t\}\ \cup\ \{T_{e}\leq t,\ \Psi_{e}(h_{T_{e}},T_{e},X_{e},R_{e})\text{ is rejection}\}.

Its probability is Se​(t)S_{e}(t). The sole arrival time is integrated once; no independence of decisions at counterfactual times is asserted. A label accepted at time tit_{i} with mark mim_{i} contributes the event density νei,hti,ti​(d​mi)​d​ti\nu_{e_{i},h_{t_{i}},t_{i}}(dm_{i})\,dt_{i}. Once the path is fixed, these are constraints on independent per-label triples. Scanning actual arrivals in order shows that the constraints are also sufficient to realize that path.

In the process with the claimed intensities, −d​log⁡Se​(u)=νe,hu,u​(ℳ)​d​u/Se​(u)-d\log S_{e}(u)=\nu_{e,h_{u},u}(\mathcal{M})\,du/S_{e}(u) before ee is accepted. The survival factor is Se​(t)S_{e}(t) for an absent label. For an accepted label it is Se​(ti)S_{e}(t_{i}), which cancels the denominator in its event intensity. Thus the two processes have the same marked-path densities. There are at most nn events, so these densities determine their laws. ∎

For analysis, include the credited value and the complete candidate realization in each acceptance mark. The other coordinates of that realization come from the accepting label’s private tape; they are not other labels’ actual values. Thus the preceding factorization still applies. Write ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} for the filtration generated by the accepted marks, that is, the information they reveal through time tt. The implemented state only needs the recorded bases. All kernels below use the prefix before a decision, or equivalently their left limits at an event time.

Set

Λe​(t)=λ​∫0tke​(u)​𝑑u.\Lambda_{e}(t)=\lambda\int_{0}^{t}k_{e}(u)\,du.

Since 2​q≥12q\geq 1, a raw early probe finds ee live with probability Λe​(t)/2\Lambda_{e}(t)/2. The Poisson test passes with probability e−Λe​(t)e^{-\Lambda_{e}(t)}. Hence the actual acceptance kernel on candidate realizations is λ​e−Λe​(t)​𝒦e,t\lambda e^{-\Lambda_{e}(t)}\mathcal{K}_{e,t} in the early phase, and λ​𝒦e,t\lambda\mathcal{K}_{e,t} in the late phase. Mapping each candidate realization to its acceptance mark gives the kernel in Lemma 18. For labels not yet accepted, that lemma gives

Se​(t)={e−Λe​(t),t≤t0,e−Λe​(t0)−λ​∫t0tke​(u)​du,t>t0.S_{e}(t)=\begin{cases}e^{-\Lambda_{e}(t)},&t\leq t_{0},\\[2.84526pt] e^{-\Lambda_{e}(t_{0})}-\lambda\displaystyle\int_{t_{0}}^{t}k_{e}(u)\,du,&t>t_{0}.\end{cases}

5.4 Persistence and the overlap gain

Lemma 19 (Persistence).

If the marked acceptance intensities are re​(t)​𝒦e,tr_{e}(t)\mathcal{K}_{e,t} and re​(t)≤Rr_{e}(t)\leq R throughout an interval, every live pair has conditional death rate at most RR, where the death rate is the instantaneous conditional rate at which the pair ceases to be live. In particular, for u≤vu\leq v in that interval,

𝔼⁡[we​(v)∣ℱu]≥e−R⁡(v−u)​we​(u).\mathbb{E}[w_{e}(v)\mid\mathcal{F}_{u}]\geq e^{-R(v-u)}w_{e}(u).

Proof.

Fix a live target pair and its current basis BB. In any source realization with current basis CC, injectivity of ϕC,B\phi_{C,B} allows at most one live source label to remove the target element. If the target label itself is live in the source, the map fixes it and no other source label can remove it. Its own acceptance is included in this bound. The killing intensity from that source realization is therefore at most R​μ​(d​y)R\mu(dy). Integration over source realizations gives the death-rate bound. Now fix a target realization live at uu. Its conditional survival probability p⁡(v)p(v) has p⁡(u)=1p(u)=1 and p′​(v)≥−R​p​(v)p^{\prime}(v)\geq-Rp(v) almost everywhere, since disappearance is irreversible. Thus p⁡(v)≥e−R⁡(v−u)p(v)\geq e^{-R(v-u)}. Integrate over live targets at uu with weight yey_{e} or 𝟏{ye>z}\mathbf{1}\{y_{e}>z\} to obtain the claim. ∎

This proof explains why the early random rejections act on whole source realizations. A bound on the total acceptance rate of each label alone would allow several labels to concentrate their mass on bases whose exchanges all evict the same target.

In the early phase the instantaneous reward rate is λ​∑ewe​(t)\lambda\sum_{e}w_{e}(t). 6 Estimating a reference instance

All quantities used by the search have a rank-layer representation. This permits a common estimator even when a large value occurs with very small probability. Sample the height of a layer in proportion to the probability that it contains an active element, then sample that layer conditioned on being nonempty. The observations are bounded in units of the expected maximum, regardless of the largest support value.

Throughout the implementation let NN denote the original ground-set size. Fix a residual matroid on n≤Nn\leq N nonloops and a reference q∈Jq\in J. Write

Vq=𝔼​maxe​Yeq,Cq=Dq−Hq.V_{q}=\mathbb{E}\max_{e}Y_{e}^{q},\qquad C_{q}=D_{q}-H_{q}.

We stop at states with zero benchmark, so Vq>0V_{q}>0 below.

6.1 Sampling a nonempty layer

Sort the distinct positive values appearing in the residual support lists as 0=v0<v1<⋯<vs0=v_{0}<v_{1}<\cdots<v_{s}. Write Δj=vj−vj−1\Delta_{j}=v_{j}-v_{j-1} and let pe,jp_{e,j} be the reference tail probability on the interval (vj−1,vj)(v_{j-1},v_{j}). In a fixed label order, form the joint weights

wj,b=Δj​pb,j​∏i<b(1−pi,j).w_{j,b}=\Delta_{j}p_{b,j}\prod_{i<b}(1-p_{i,j}).

Their sum is

∑j,bwj,b=∑jΔj​(1−∏e(1−pe,j))=Vq.\sum_{j,b}w_{j,b}=\sum_{j}\Delta_{j}\left(1-\prod_{e}(1-p_{e,j})\right)=V_{q}.

Draw (j,b)(j,b) with probability wj,b/Vqw_{j,b}/V_{q}. Set the indicators before bb to zero and the indicator of bb to one; draw each later indicator ee independently with probability pe,jp_{e,j}. Denote the resulting nonempty active set by RR. If RjR_{j} is an unconditioned product layer, then

Pr⁡((j,R))=ΔjVq​Pr⁡(Rj=R),R≠∅.\Pr((j,R))=\frac{\Delta_{j}}{V_{q}}\Pr(R_{j}=R),\qquad R\neq\varnothing. (6.1)

Indeed, RR has a unique first active label. Even when Pr⁡(Rj≠∅)\Pr(R_{j}\neq\varnothing) is small, this construction uses one categorical draw and at most nn Bernoulli draws.

Let 𝒞⁡(R)\mathcal{C}(R) be the coloops of M|RM|_{R}. From this one layer form

ZF\displaystyle Z_{F} =Vq​r​(R),\displaystyle=V_{q}r(R), ZD\displaystyle Z_{D} =Vq​|𝒞⁡(R)|,\displaystyle=V_{q}|\mathcal{C}(R)|,
ZC\displaystyle Z_{C} =Vq​∑e∈𝒞⁡(R)(1−pe,j),\displaystyle=V_{q}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{C}(R)}(1-p_{e,j}), Ze\displaystyle Z_{e} =Vq𝟏{e∈cl(R∖e)}.\displaystyle=V_{q}\mathbf{1}\{e\in\operatorname{cl}(R\setminus e)\}.
Lemma 20 (Common layer estimates).

The expectations of ZF,ZD,ZC,ZeZ_{F},Z_{D},Z_{C},Z_{e} are Fq,Dq,Cq,meqF_{q},D_{q},C_{q},m_{e}^{q}, respectively. On every outcome,

Vq≤ZF≤N​Vq,0≤ZC≤ZD≤ZF,0≤Ze≤Vq.V_{q}\leq Z_{F}\leq NV_{q},\qquad 0\leq Z_{C}\leq Z_{D}\leq Z_{F},\qquad 0\leq Z_{e}\leq V_{q}.

All observations can be computed with O⁡(n​log⁡(n+1))O(n\log(n+1)) independence queries.

The rank layer formula gives the first expectation. An active element is a coloop of the active restriction exactly when the other active elements do not span it. Thus the unconditioned expectations of the next two layer statistics are ∑epe​ρe\sum_{e}p_{e}\rho_{e} and ∑epe​(1−pe)​ρe\sum_{e}p_{e}(1-p_{e})\rho_{e}, where ρe=Pr⁡(e∉cl⁡(Rj∖e))\rho_{e}=\Pr(e\notin\operatorname{cl}(R_{j}\setminus e)). meq=∫0∞Pr⁡(e∈cl⁡(Rz∖e))​𝑑z.m_{e}^{q}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(e\in\operatorname{cl}(R_{z}\setminus e))\,dz.

For the query bound, greedily find a basis BB of RR and initialize U=BU=B. For f∈R∖Bf\in R\setminus B, its fundamental circuit CfC_{f} satisfies

(B∖S)+f is independent⟺Cf∩S≠∅(S⊆B).(B\setminus S)+f\text{ is independent}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C_{f}\cap S\neq\varnothing\qquad(S\subseteq B).

7 Choosing the reference parameter

A small additive error in the reference potential could accumulate over many arrivals. We avoid this loss by moving the reference only when the samples certify the sign of a one-sided derivative. At the returned point we need just two inequalities relating the deletion surplus to the stable surplus.

Write

g⁡(q)=a⁡(q)​Fq,d∗​(q)=θ​q1−θ​q.g(q)=a(q)F_{q},\qquad d_{*}(q)=\frac{\theta q}{1-\theta q}.

Lemma 9 gives concavity of gg. Since a′=−θa^{\prime}=-\theta, Lemma 8 gives

a​Fqq​(CqFq−d∗​(q))≤g+′​(q)≤g−′​(q)≤a​Fqq​(DqFq−d∗​(q)).\frac{aF_{q}}{q}\left(\frac{C_{q}}{F_{q}}-d_{*}(q)\right)\leq g^{\prime}_{+}(q)\leq g^{\prime}_{-}(q)\leq\frac{aF_{q}}{q}\left(\frac{D_{q}}{F_{q}}-d_{*}(q)\right). (7.1)

At an evaluated parameter call the batch positive if C^/F^>d∗+10​ε\widehat{C}/\widehat{F}>d_{*}+10\varepsilon, and negative if D^/F^<d∗−10​ε\widehat{D}/\widehat{F}<d_{*}-10\varepsilon. These tests are disjoint, since 0≤C^≤D^≤F^0\leq\widehat{C}\leq\widehat{D}\leq\widehat{F} on every outcome. The denominator is positive because F^≥Vq\widehat{F}\geq V_{q}.

Initialize the search at the inherited qinq^{\rm in}, where |qin−1|<3​δ|q^{\rm in}-1|<3\delta. Evaluate this parameter. If neither test holds, return it and its batch. If its batch is positive, bisect [qin,1+4​δ][q^{\rm in},1+4\delta]: a positive midpoint replaces the left endpoint and its saved batch, and any other midpoint replaces the right endpoint. Return the saved left endpoint. If its batch is negative, use the symmetric procedure on [1−4​δ,qin][1-4\delta,q^{\rm in}] and return the saved right endpoint. In either branch perform K−1K-1 midpoint evaluations, where

K=1+⌈log2⁡max⁡{1,32​δ​N2ε}⌉.K=1+\left\lceil\log_{2}\max\left\{1,\frac{32\delta N^{2}}{\varepsilon}\right\}\right\rceil. (7.2)

The terminal interval has length at most ε/(4​N2)<δ\varepsilon/(4N^{2})<\delta.

Lemma 22 (Reference selection).

On the simultaneous accurate event, the returned reference satisfies

a⁡(q)​Fq≥a⁡(qin)​Fqin.a(q)F_{q}\geq a(q^{\rm in})F_{q^{\rm in}}.

If |q−1|<3​δ|q-1|<3\delta, then

d∗​(q)−20​ε≤Dq/Fq≤d∗​(q)+Hq/Fq+20​ε.d_{*}(q)-20\varepsilon\leq D_{q}/F_{q}\leq d_{*}(q)+H_{q}/F_{q}+20\varepsilon. (7.3)

Proof.

Accuracy and Cq,Dq≤FqC_{q},D_{q}\leq F_{q} imply that both estimated ratios differ from their true ratios by at most 4​ε/(1−2​ε)≤5​ε4\varepsilon/(1-2\varepsilon)\leq 5\varepsilon. Thus a positive batch certifies g+′>0g^{\prime}_{+}>0, and a negative batch certifies g−′<0g^{\prime}_{-}<0. By concavity, a parameter with a positive batch has larger potential than every point to its left, and a parameter with a negative batch has larger potential than every point to its right. Every update to the saved endpoint therefore increases the potential.

The two endpoints of the final interval may have different test outcomes. To transfer a failed test across that interval, we bound how fast its true ratio can change. Put q−=1−4​δ≥1/2q_{-}=1-4\delta\geq 1/2 and a−=minJ⁡a≥1/2a_{-}=\min_{J}a\geq 1/2. Coupling the product layers at two parameters gives

|Dq−Ds|≤n2​F1​|q−s|,|Hq−Hs|≤2​n2​F1​|q−s|,|Cq−Cs|≤3​n2​F1​|q−s|.|D_{q}-D_{s}|\leq n^{2}F_{1}|q-s|,\quad|H_{q}-H_{s}|\leq 2n^{2}F_{1}|q-s|,\quad|C_{q}-C_{s}|\leq 3n^{2}F_{1}|q-s|.

In the positive branch the saved left endpoint is certified positive. If the final right endpoint is interior, it was assigned by a failed positive test, so its true normalized CC ratio is at most 15​ε15\varepsilon above d∗d_{*}. The negative branch is symmetric. All ratio tests can be performed by cross multiplication. The estimates share the factor Vq/mV_{q}/m, and every new parameter is a midpoint of two old endpoints. Appendix C uses these facts to bound the bit complexity of the search.

8 The online algorithm and its guarantee

The selected reference serves two purposes. Its location and its stable surplus determine whether the virtual continuation can earn the entire remaining potential. If the algorithm instead takes a threshold step, the same reference supplies a price for each possible next arrival.

8.1 Conditions on the parameters

The three inequalities below correspond to the two ways of entering the continuation and the single threshold step. Put

h−=η−10ε,h+=η+10ε,b=b(q)=a(q)1+ε1−ε,z∗​(q)=h−21−d∗​(q)+20​ε+h−,L∗​(q)=1−b+bb+s​(d∗​(q)+20​ε−(1−b)−b​e−s).\begin{gathered}h_{-}=\eta-10\varepsilon,\qquad h_{+}=\eta+10\varepsilon,\qquad b=b(q)=a(q)\frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon},\\ z_{*}(q)=\frac{h_{-}^{2}}{1-d_{*}(q)+20\varepsilon+h_{-}},\\ L_{*}(q)=1-b+\frac{b}{b+s}\left(d_{*}(q)+20\varepsilon-(1-b)-be^{-s}\right).\end{gathered} (8.1)

The elementary restrictions (4.2) make the denominator of z∗z_{*} positive and give 0<b<10<b<1. In addition to ω>0\omega>0 and q⁡(b+s)>1q(b+s)>1 throughout JJ, require

Φδ​(q,0)\displaystyle\Phi_{\delta}(q,0) ≥a⁡(q)\displaystyle\geq a(q) if ​q∈J,|q−1|≥3​δ,\displaystyle\text{if }q\in J,\ |q-1|\geq 3\delta, (8.2)
Φδ​(q,z∗​(q))\displaystyle\Phi_{\delta}(q,z_{*}(q)) ≥a⁡(q)\displaystyle\geq a(q) for ​q∈J,\displaystyle\text{for }q\in J, (8.3)
L∗​(q)\displaystyle L_{*}(q) >b​q​(d∗​(q)+h++20​ε)+2​ε\displaystyle>bq\bigl(d_{*}(q)+h_{+}+20\varepsilon\bigr)+2\varepsilon if ​|q−1|≤3​δ.\displaystyle\text{if }|q-1|\leq 3\delta. (8.4)

The first condition covers a reference close to the edge of the search interval. The second pays for a continuation with large stable surplus. The third pays for a threshold step when stable surplus is small. Appendix D verifies these conditions simultaneously.

8.2 The policy

If AA is the set of accepted elements and RR the set of rejected or discarded elements, the residual matroid is (M0/A)∖R(M_{0}/A)\setminus R. At each decision, the algorithm computes the reference and all prices before revealing the next remaining label. The value of NN in the error allowances stays fixed throughout.

A loop is ignored when it arrives. Conditional on the history, the relative order of the remaining nonloops is uniform and their values retain their original product law. Reference samples are independent of these future arrivals. A threshold acceptance preserves feasibility by contraction. At entry to a virtual continuation we use the current minor and the selected reference, initialize its local accepted set and record list to be empty, and attach fresh sorted clocks to the remaining arrivals as in Section 5.

Each threshold step removes one label. There are therefore at most NN searches and at most one virtual continuation. A reference passed to another search always satisfies |q−1|<3​δ|q-1|<3\delta. When N=0N=0, the algorithm returns the empty set before using NN in a denominator.

8.3 One-step progress

Lemma 23 (Local potential bound).

Assume (4.2) and (8.2)–(8.4), as well as ω>0\omega>0 and q⁡(b+s)>1q(b+s)>1 throughout JJ. At a positive-value residual state, on the event that all queried batches are accurate, the next action has expected reward plus continuation potential at least

a⁡(qin)​Fqin.a(q^{\rm in})F_{q^{\rm in}}.

After a threshold step, the potential is evaluated on the child minor at the inherited selected parameter qq. A virtual continuation has zero terminal potential.

Fix all queried batches at the state and write qq for the selected reference. Abbreviate a=a⁡(q)a=a(q), F=FqF=F_{q}, D=DqD=D_{q}, and H=HqH=H_{q}. Reference selection gives a​F≥a⁡(qin)​FqinaF\geq a(q^{\rm in})F_{q^{\rm in}}, so it suffices to pay for a​FaF.

If |q−1|≥3​δ|q-1|\geq 3\delta, the continuation earns at least a​FaF by Proposition 16, Q≥0Q\geq 0, and (8.2). It remains to consider |q−1|<3​δ|q-1|<3\delta. Reference selection then gives

d∗−20​ε≤D/F≤d∗+H/F+20​ε.d_{*}-20\varepsilon\leq D/F\leq d_{*}+H/F+20\varepsilon. (8.5)

The two ratio estimates used by the search also imply

|D^−C^F^−HF|≤10​ε.\left|\frac{\widehat{D}-\widehat{C}}{\widehat{F}}-\frac{H}{F}\right|\leq 10\varepsilon.

8.4 Charging statistical errors

Proposition 24 (Guarantee with exact random primitives).

Under the stated parameter conditions, the ideal policy satisfies

𝔼⁡[ALG]≥(1−θ−ρ)​F0.\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]\geq(1-\theta-\rho)F_{0}.

Its expected number of matroid independence queries is O⁡(N4)O(N^{4}).

Proof.

If F0=0F_{0}=0, the policy stops and the claim is immediate. Otherwise use the potential 𝒫⁡(M,q)=a⁡(q)​Fq​(M)\mathcal{P}(M,q)=a(q)F_{q}(M). Initially it is (1−θ)​F0(1-\theta)F_{0}. For every residual minor, F1​(M)≤F0F_{1}(M)\leq F_{0}, so Lemma 8 and (4.2) imply

0≤𝒫⁡(M,q)≤(maxu∈J⁡a⁡(u))​q+​F1​(M)≤F0.0\leq\mathcal{P}(M,q)\leq\bigl(\max_{u\in J}a(u)\bigr)q_{+}F_{1}(M)\leq F_{0}.

Conditionally at each computation state, all queried batches are accurate with probability at least 1−ρ/N1-\rho/N, by Lemma 21. On that event, Lemma 23 gives nonnegative expected drift of reward plus potential. On the complementary event, rewards and subsequent potentials remain nonnegative, so the expected decrease is at most F0F_{0}.

Treat a virtual continuation as one final epoch and append empty epochs to obtain exactly NN epochs. Summing conditional drift bounds loses at most N⁡(ρ/N)​F0=ρ​F0N(\rho/N)F_{0}=\rho F_{0}. No union bound over possible residual minors is needed.

There are at most N​K​m=O⁡(N2​log2⁡(N+2))NKm=O(N^{2}\log^{2}(N+2)) layer samples. Their total query cost is O⁡(N3​log3⁡(N+2))O(N^{3}\log^{3}(N+2)). Loop detection and actual decisions use O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) further queries. The one possible virtual continuation costs O⁡(N4)O(N^{4}) in expectation. Since log3⁡(N+2)=O⁡(N)\log^{3}(N+2)=O(N), the total is O⁡(N4)O(N^{4}). ∎

Appendix C converts this policy to a bounded-bit algorithm at an additional loss of at most ρ​F0\rho F_{0}. The resulting competitive ratio is 1−θ−2​ρ1-\theta-2\rho.

9 The sharp bound for XOS valuations

We now turn from selecting elements of a matroid to allocating disjoint bundles to buyers. For XOS valuations, Ehsani et al. [EHKS18] give a 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee. We prove the matching upper bound even when every buyer draws her valuation from the same distribution. Our instance has a simple description. Each buyer values the items she receives in one part of a partition, and her type specifies which parts she may use. The prophet can usually choose a single partition that serves all buyers. An online algorithm must allocate each bundle before it knows which partition will serve the later buyers.

9.1 A family of partitions

Fix n≥2n\geq 2 buyers and a finite index set 𝒯\mathcal{T}. An item is a function from 𝒯\mathcal{T} to [n][n], so the item set is M=[n]𝒯M=[n]^{\mathcal{T}} and m=|M|=n|𝒯|m=|M|=n^{|\mathcal{T}|}. Each coordinate s∈𝒯s\in\mathcal{T} partitions MM into the nn equal parts

Psr={x∈M:x⁡(s)=r},r∈[n].P_{s}^{r}=\{x\in M:x(s)=r\},\qquad r\in[n].

All these partitions are public. Within a partition the nn parts are disjoint. Across partitions their overlaps are given by the product rule.

Lemma 25 (Counting partition parts).

For distinct s1,…,sk∈𝒯s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}\in\mathcal{T} and arbitrary r1,…,rk∈[n]r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}\in[n],

|⋃i=1kPsiri|=m⁡(1−(1−1n)k).\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}P_{s_{i}}^{r_{i}}\right|=m\left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^{k}\right).
Proof.

Outside the union each of the kk specified coordinates has n−1n-1 possible values. Each of the other coordinates has nn possibilities. ∎

9.2 An i.i.d. distribution of buyer types

Fix L≥nL\geq n and index the partitions by 𝒯=([L]n)\mathcal{T}=\binom{[L]}{n}. Give each buyer an independent uniform label in [L][L]. For any partition index ss containing her label aa, she may use part rs​(a)r_{s}(a), where rs​(a)r_{s}(a) is the position of aa in the increasing order on ss. Her valuation for a bundle SS is

va(S)=maxs∈𝒯:a∈s|S∩Psrs​(a)|.v^{a}(S)=\max_{s\in\mathcal{T}:\,a\in s}|S\cap P_{s}^{r_{s}(a)}|. (9.1)

This is the maximum of additive clauses with coefficients in {0,1}\{0,1\}. In particular,

va​(S)≤|S|,va​(M)=m/n.v^{a}(S)\leq|S|,\qquad v^{a}(M)=m/n. (9.2)

The prophet.

If the nn labels are distinct, their set is a partition index ss. Allocating the part Psrs​(a)P_{s}^{r_{s}(a)} to each buyer with label aa assigns every item exactly once, for welfare mm. A pair of labels coincides with probability 1/L1/L. Thus

𝔼⁡[OPT]≥m⁡(1−(n2)/L).\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}]\geq m\left(1-\binom{n}{2}/L\right). (9.3)

The online allocation.

Reveal the entire permutation of buyer identities in advance and the label of each buyer at her arrival. Conditional on the permutation and the algorithm’s independent random tape, the labels A1,…,AnA_{1},\ldots,A_{n} in arrival order remain independent and uniform. When the algorithm gives StS_{t} to the buyer at position tt, fix the first maximizing index WtW_{t} in a public ordering of the clauses in (9.1). Then

At∈Wt,vAt​(St)=|St∩PWtrWt​(At)|.A_{t}\in W_{t},\qquad v^{A_{t}}(S_{t})=|S_{t}\cap P_{W_{t}}^{r_{W_{t}}(A_{t})}|. (9.4)

We can fix this witness at the moment of allocation, even if several clauses attain the same value. For t<ut<u, the witnesses can coincide only if the future label AuA_{u} lies in the already fixed nn-set WtW_{t}. Conditional on the history through tt, that event has probability n/Ln/L. A union bound gives

Pr[∃t<u:Wt=Wu]≤(n2)nL.\Pr[\exists\,t<u:\ W_{t}=W_{u}]\leq\binom{n}{2}\frac{n}{L}. (9.5)

When all witnesses are distinct, the nn credited sets in (9.4) are disjoint subsets of their respective partition parts. Hence, by Lemma 25, their total size is at most m​cnmc_{n}, where cn=1−(1−1/n)nc_{n}=1-(1-1/n)^{n}. This counting identity holds for every choice of distinct indices, including the ones selected by the algorithm’s past decisions. On a collision the welfare is at most mm by (9.2). Averaging over the permutation and the random tape gives

𝔼⁡[ALG]≤m⁡(cn+n​(n2)/L).\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]\leq m\left(c_{n}+n\binom{n}{2}/L\right). (9.6)
Proof of Theorem 3.

For L>(n2)L>\binom{n}{2}, dividing (9.6) by the lower bound in (9.3) gives

𝔼⁡[ALG]𝔼⁡[OPT]≤cn+n​(n2)/L1−(n2)/L.\frac{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{ALG}]}{\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{OPT}]}\leq\frac{c_{n}+n\binom{n}{2}/L}{1-\binom{n}{2}/L}. (9.7)

Given ξ>0\xi>0, choose nn so that cn<1−1/e+ξ/2c_{n}<1-1/e+\xi/2 and then LL so that the right-hand side is below 1−1/e+ξ1-1/e+\xi. These choices work for every online algorithm. ∎

The bound allows unlimited computation and full knowledge of the input law. Indeed the list of clauses, over all LL possible types, has L​(L−1n−1)=n​|𝒯|L\binom{L-1}{n-1}=n|\mathcal{T}| clause occurrences. Listing the mm binary coefficients of each takes n​m​logn⁡mnm\log_{n}m bits. The uncertainty is about which types will arrive.

Corollary 26.

For 0<ξ<1/40<\xi<1/4, the instance in Theorem 3 can have O⁡(ξ−4​log⁡(1/ξ))O(\xi^{-4}\log(1/\xi)) items.

Proof.

Set c=1−1/ec=1-1/e, n=1+⌈8/ξ⌉n=1+\lceil 8/\xi\rceil, and L=⌈8​n3/ξ⌉L=\lceil 8n^{3}/\xi\rceil. Sample m′m^{\prime} items independently from MM, treating repeated samples as distinct items. Restrict each clause to these items. For any fixed choice of nn distinct partition indices and one part from each, the fraction of sampled items in their union is the mean of m′m^{\prime} independent Bernoulli variables of mean cnc_{n}. Let ζ=ξ/8\zeta=\xi/8 and take m′=⌈(1+n​log⁡(n​|𝒯|))/(2​ζ2)⌉m^{\prime}=\lceil(1+n\log(n|\mathcal{T}|))/(2\zeta^{2})\rceil. Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound over at most (n​|𝒯|)n(n|\mathcal{T}|)^{n} choices give a realization in which every such union covers at most a cn+ζc_{n}+\zeta fraction. Fix this realization and make it public.

Every partition still covers all m′m^{\prime} items, so the prophet earns m′m^{\prime} whenever the labels are distinct. The collision bound (9.5) still holds because each witness is indexed by a set of nn types. Consequently (9.7) holds with cn+ζc_{n}+\zeta in place of cnc_{n}. The power series for log⁡(1−1/n)\log(1-1/n) gives n​log⁡(1−1/n)≥−1−1/(2​(n−1))n\log(1-1/n)\geq-1-1/(2(n-1)), whence cn−c≤1/(2​e​(n−1))<ξ/16c_{n}-c\leq 1/(2e(n-1))<\xi/16. Also n​(n2)/L<ξ/16n\binom{n}{2}/L<\xi/16. The ratio is therefore at most (c+ξ/4)/(1−ξ/16)<c+ξ(c+\xi/4)/(1-\xi/16)<c+\xi. Finally, |𝒯|≤Ln|\mathcal{T}|\leq L^{n} gives the stated bound on m′m^{\prime}. The number of clauses per valuation can still be exponential in nn. ∎

9.3 Relation to coverage welfare

The upper bound also follows from Udwani and Wajc’s theorem for online coverage welfare under known i.i.d. item arrivals [UW26, Theorem 1.2]. We give the reduction to clarify the change of arrival model. It uses the coverage-to-XOS construction of Chawla and Dang [CD26, Appendix D], who apply it to allocation with free disposal.

In the coverage problem there are kk fixed buyers. Buyer aa has a universe UaU_{a} with nonnegative weights wa,uw_{a,u}, and an arriving item of type ee covers Ca,e⊆UaC_{a,e}\subseteq U_{a} if assigned to her. Her value is the total weight of the union of sets covered by her assigned items. Take disjoint copies of the universes. In the auction their elements become the items. Each arrival of type ee becomes a buyer with valuation

ve​(S)=max⁡∑u∈S∩Ca,ea∈[k]⁡wa,u.v_{e}(S)=\max_{a\in[k]}\sum_{u\in S\cap C_{a,e}}w_{a,u}. (9.8)

To simulate an auction algorithm in the coverage problem, assign the arriving item to a maximizing clause aa for the bundle SS it allocates. All elements counted in that clause are then covered by buyer aa. Because the auction bundles are disjoint, these elements are charged at most once across arrivals. The coverage welfare therefore dominates the auction welfare. Conversely, whenever a coverage algorithm assigns ee to aa, give the corresponding auction buyer the elements of Ca,eC_{a,e} still unallocated. They are exactly the elements newly covered by this assignment, and the bundle earns their total weight. Both simulations run online. Applied offline they give equality of the optima. Finally, i.i.d. item types induce i.i.d. buyer valuations, whose joint law is preserved by an independent random permutation. Thus the information-theoretic coverage upper bound transfers to this auction model.

Appendix A Implementing the common-law rule

Let n=|E⁡(M)|≥1n=|E(M)|\geq 1. An independence query to MM costs TIT_{I}, and a query returning F⁡(x−)F(x-) and F⁡(x)F(x) costs TFT_{F}. We first count arithmetic operations, comparisons, and uniform draws on [0,1][0,1] at unit cost. We give the finite-bit version below. Let II be the accepted set. To test whether A⊆E⁡(N)∖{e}A\subseteq E(N)\setminus\{e\} spans ee, greedily extend II through AA, then test whether the resulting independent set can be augmented by ee. The test takes at most |A|+1|A|+1 queries. Applying it to the empty set and the whole remaining set detects loops and coloops.

Proposition 27.

For an absolute constant CC, using m=⌈C​n2​⌈log2⁡(2​n)⌉⌉m=\lceil Cn^{2}\lceil\log_{2}(2n)\rceil\rceil trials per arrival in Algorithm 3 gives competitive ratio c0c_{0}. The running time is O⁡(n4​log⁡(2​n)​(1+TI)+n​TF)O(n^{4}\log(2n)(1+T_{I})+nT_{F}).

The sampling error would cost a small additive term if we used only the guarantee in Theorem 4. On a ground set of size nn, however, the comparison has slack of order 1/n1/n. We prove this first and then use the slack to pay for sampling.

Proof.

Let g⁡(a)=e−1−a/ag(a)=e^{-1-a}/a. Consider a deterministic cutoff qq calibrated at S⁡(q)=e−aS(q)=e^{-a} with η0/2≤a≤3​η0/2\eta_{0}/2\leq a\leq 3\eta_{0}/2, for a label that is neither a loop nor a coloop. There are absolute constants K,B>0K,B>0 with

D⁡(v)min⁡(q,v)≤1+η0+K​|a−η0|−B/n(0<v≤1).\frac{D(v)}{\min(q,v)}\leq 1+\eta_{0}+K|a-\eta_{0}|-B/n\qquad(0<v\leq 1). (A.1)

Indeed, the event of sampling no other label gives S⁡(q)≥(1−q)n−1S(q)\geq(1-q)^{n-1}. Thus q≥1−e−a/(n−1)≥b/nq\geq 1-e^{-a/(n-1)}\geq b/n for b=1−e−η0/2b=1-e^{-\eta_{0}/2}. Set d=1−q/τ⁡(q)d=1-q/\tau(q). Since τ⁡(q)≥q+q2/2\tau(q)\geq q+q^{2}/2, we have d≥q/3d\geq q/3. For v≤qv\leq q, Lemma 5 gives 1−S⁡(v)≤a​τ​(v)/τ⁡(q)1-S(v)\leq a\tau(v)/\tau(q). Corollary 28 (Explicit rational distributions).

Appendix B Optimal quantile cutoffs in uniform random order

The common-law algorithm in Section 3 works for every fixed arrival order independent of the draws. With a uniform permutation we can characterize the best guarantee for each individual matroid without imposing a local comparison. Fix a matroid MM of positive rank on nn labels, and let VM​(F)V_{M}(F) be the value of its optimal online policy in uniform random order. Write

γ(M)=infF:PM​(F)>0VM​(F)PM​(F),\gamma(M)=\inf_{F:P_{M}(F)>0}\frac{V_{M}(F)}{P_{M}(F)},

where FF ranges over nonnegative common laws of finite mean. The policy inside the infimum may use the entire law. The next theorem shows that one table of quantile cutoffs, chosen knowing only the matroid, achieves γ⁡(M)\gamma(M) simultaneously for all common laws.

A flow on minors.

Make a vertex for each residual labeled minor NN. The root MM has mass one. If a nonempty NN receives mass yNy_{N}, the mass at which ee arrives next is bN​e=yN/|E⁡(N)|b_{Ne}=y_{N}/|E(N)|. Send aN​ea_{Ne} units of this mass to N/eN/e and bN​e−aN​eb_{Ne}-a_{Ne} to N∖eN\setminus e, with 0≤aN​e≤bN​e0\leq a_{Ne}\leq b_{Ne} and aN​e=0a_{Ne}=0 for loops. Sum the incoming masses at each vertex, including both arcs if they reach the same child. The graph is acyclic, and the feasible flows form a compact polytope 𝒟M\mathcal{D}_{M}. A flow DD prescribes a cutoff qN​e=aN​e/bN​eq_{Ne}=a_{Ne}/b_{Ne} at every positive-mass arrival. Put

TD​(v)=∑N,emin⁡(aN​e,v​bN​e).T_{D}(v)=\sum_{N,e}\min(a_{Ne},vb_{Ne}).
Theorem 29 (Simultaneous quantile cutoffs).

In uniform random order,

γ⁡(M)=max⁡inf0<v≤1D∈𝒟M⁡TD​(v)RM​(v).\gamma(M)=\max_{D\in\mathcal{D}_{M}}\inf_{0<v\leq 1}\frac{T_{D}(v)}{R_{M}(v)}.

The quantile cutoffs of a maximizing flow attain this ratio for every common law.

Proof.

Any adaptive policy induces a feasible flow. Conditional on the past, the next label is uniform on the unseen labels, and the arriving quantile is fresh. Of the total mass bN​eb_{Ne}, at most aN​ea_{Ne} is accepted and at most v​bN​evb_{Ne} belongs to the top vv quantile band. Accepting its best qN​eq_{Ne} fraction attains the minimum of the two. This change preserves the masses of both children, so by induction it realizes the entire flow and earns exactly TD​(v)T_{D}(v) on every band. Zero-mass states can use arbitrary feasible decisions. It follows by integration over weight levels that any flow satisfying TD​(v)≥c​RM​(v)T_{D}(v)\geq cR_{M}(v) for all vv is cc-competitive on every law.

It remains to find such a flow for c=γ⁡(M)c=\gamma(M). Fix finitely many positive endpoints v1,…,vkv_{1},\ldots,v_{k}. The set of vectors dominated coordinatewise by (TD​(vi))i(T_{D}(v_{i}))_{i} for some DD is closed by compactness and convex by concavity of each TD​(vi)T_{D}(v_{i}) in DD. If this set excluded (c​RM​(vi))i(cR_{M}(v_{i}))_{i}, strict separation from that point by a hyperplane would give coefficients λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0, not all zero, with

max⁡∑iD∈𝒟M⁡λi​TD​(vi)<c​∑iλi​RM​(vi).\max_{D\in\mathcal{D}_{M}}\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}T_{D}(v_{i})<c\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}R_{M}(v_{i}).

For example, the deficit RM​(v)−TD​(v)R_{M}(v)-T_{D}(v) is the sum over nonloop arrivals of positive mass of

bN​e​[(qN​e−v)+​(1−SeN​(v))+(v−qN​e)+​SeN​(v)].b_{Ne}\bigl[(q_{Ne}-v)_{+}(1-S_{e}^{N}(v))+(v-q_{Ne})_{+}S_{e}^{N}(v)\bigr].

Finite approximation.

For 0<δ≤10<\delta\leq 1, start at v1=δ/nv_{1}=\delta/n, increase the endpoints by a factor 1+δ1+\delta, and append 11 as the last endpoint. On this grid maximize cc subject to the flow constraints and

The flow follows minors under a particular policy. A different identity compares the optimal policy and the prophet on the same random restrictions. Let μ=𝔼​X\mu=\mathbb{E}X and ϕ⁡(t)=𝔼​(X−t)+\phi(t)=\mathbb{E}(X-t)_{+}. For a nonloop ee of a minor NN, define

For the uniform label in Nℓ​sN_{\ell s},

𝔼​we\displaystyle\mathbb{E}w_{e} =vℓ+1,s−vℓ+1,s+1,\displaystyle=v_{\ell+1,s}-v_{\ell+1,s+1},
vℓ​s−vℓ+1,s\displaystyle v_{\ell s}-v_{\ell+1,s} =Pr⁡(e​ is a coloop)​μ+𝔼⁡[𝟏Ae​ϕ​(we)].\displaystyle=\Pr(e\text{ is a coloop})\mu+\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{A_{e}}\phi(w_{e})].
