Appendix C Finite precision and polynomial running time

We now implement the ideal policy with a deterministic bound on all random-bit and arithmetic work. The distributions are explicit lists of nonnegative rational values and rational probabilities. Let LL be their total binary encoding length and sins_{\rm in} the number of support entries. Zero-probability entries may be removed. The parameters are fixed rational constants; choose δ\delta dyadic, as in Appendix D.

The statistical estimates cost at most ρ​F0\rho F_{0} in expected reward. We give the implementation an additional budget of ρ​F0\rho F_{0}. A uniform coupling conditional on the actual values will let us charge an implementation discrepancy to the realized offline optimum.

C.1 Rational encodings

Let DXD_{X} and DvD_{v} be the products of the input probability and value denominators, respectively. Their bit lengths are O⁡(L)O(L). At a queried reference q=u/wq=u/w, every reference tail and atom probability has denominator dividing dp=w​DXd_{p}=wD_{X}. Every joint layer weight can be placed over the common denominator Dv​dpnD_{v}d_{p}^{n}, so

Vq=vDv​dpnV_{q}=\frac{v}{D_{v}d_{p}^{n}}

for an integer vv of polynomial bit length. Thus the joint sampling table has at most N​sinNs_{\rm in} entries, all of polynomial encoding length. Very small probabilities do not create a dependence on their reciprocals.

The averages can be accumulated using integer counters:

F^=Vqm​kF,D^=Vqm​kD,m^e=Vqm​ke,C^=Vqm​dp​kC.\widehat{F}=\frac{V_{q}}{m}k_{F},\quad\widehat{D}=\frac{V_{q}}{m}k_{D},\quad\widehat{m}_{e}=\frac{V_{q}}{m}k_{e},\quad\widehat{C}=\frac{V_{q}}{md_{p}}k_{C}.

Here kF,kD≤m​Nk_{F},k_{D}\leq mN, ke≤mk_{e}\leq m, and kC≤m​N​dpk_{C}\leq mNd_{p}. For the last counter, a sampled coloop contributes the integer dp​(1−pe,j)d_{p}(1-p_{e,j}). Thus averaging mm samples adds only O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m) bits. The affine discount and thresholds have polynomial encoding length.

If the denominator of δ\delta is 2d2^{d}, every parameter formed by at most N​KNK midpoint operations has denominator dividing 2d+N​K2^{d+NK}. Thus its encoding length is O⁡(d+N​K)O(d+NK), independently of the numerical estimates. The input distributions on surviving labels never change. Thus the encodings have polynomial length over the entire run.

C.2 A bounded categorical primitive

Let S=N​K​mS=NKm, which bounds all layer samples on every execution. Set

T=⌈log2⁡8​Nρ⌉,Ccat=S⁡(N+2)+N2​(1+T)+2​N+N​T,J0=N​sin+N+T+3.T=\left\lceil\log_{2}\frac{8N}{\rho}\right\rceil,\qquad C_{\rm cat}=S(N+2)+N^{2}(1+T)+2N+NT,\qquad J_{0}=Ns_{\rm in}+N+T+3.

Choose G=2ℓbitG=2^{\ell_{\rm bit}} so that

G​δ∈ℤ,G≥2​(4​N2+Ccat​J0)ρ.G\delta\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad G\geq\frac{2(4N^{2}+C_{\rm cat}J_{0})}{\rho}. (C.1)

Every auxiliary draw uses exactly ℓbit\ell_{\rm bit} fair bits to obtain an integer JJ uniform on {0,…,G−1}\{0,\ldots,G-1\}.

For rational category probabilities p1,…,pkp_{1},\ldots,p_{k}, form their cumulative sums and return the first ii for which ∑j≤ipj>J/G\sum_{j\leq i}p_{j}>J/G. This uses exact rational comparisons. Zero-probability categories are never returned. The primitive covers reference coordinates, layer choices, Bernoulli screens, and probe prefixes.

For an arrival in the early phase of the continuation, draw the probe count from {0,…,T}\{0,\ldots,T\} with probabilities proportional to the rational weights 2k/k!2^{k}/k!. These are the probabilities of a Poisson random variable of mean two conditioned to be at most TT. They may be represented by the integer weights 2k​T!/k!2^{k}T!/k!. The implementation therefore requires neither exact exponential evaluations nor an unbounded count sampler.

Arrival clocks use the one-based grid (J+1)/G(J+1)/G: draw one clock for each residual label, sort them, and assign them in order to the actual arrivals. For a raw probe use a fresh zero-based draw and set u=2​q​J/Gu=2qJ/G; test the corresponding prefix only when u<su<s, where ss is the current arrival clock. Keep repeated arrival clocks. Candidate realizations replay all preceding records in their append order. A probe replays the records whose clocks are at most uu, also in append order. Every candidate basis therefore contains all preceding acceptances, even on executions with equal clocks, and feasibility is unconditional.

Lemma 31 (Categorical approximation).

An exact categorical draw with kk categories and the bounded-bit draw can be coupled to disagree with probability at most (k−1)/G(k-1)/G. For ordered nonnegative integer categories the bounded-bit draw is no larger than the exact draw under this coupling.

Proof.

Use the same uniform U∈[0,1)U\in[0,1) and let J=⌊G​U⌋J=\lfloor GU\rfloor. A discrepancy requires an interior cumulative boundary between J/GJ/G and UU. Each of the k−1k-1 boundaries contributes probability at most 1/G1/G. The ordering assertion follows because J/G≤UJ/G\leq U. ∎

Lemma 32 (Uniform implementation error).

For every fixed actual value vector in the positive-probability input supports and every fixed actual arrival permutation, the ideal and finite-bit algorithms can be coupled to make identical acceptance decisions with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho. Their expected reward difference is consequently at most ρ​F0\rho F_{0}.

Proof.

First round continuous arrival clocks upward to the grid, retaining exact categorical draws and Poisson counts. The probability of a clock collision is at most n⁡(n−1)/(2​G)n(n-1)/(2G); declare a coupling failure on this event. Otherwise the clock order is preserved. Since the switching time 1−δ1-\delta is a grid point, rounding also preserves the early or late phase.

For a raw early probe, list the preceding accepted times as τ1≤⋯≤τk≤s\tau_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\tau_{k}\leq s. Its possible prefix categories have cumulative boundaries

τ12​q,…,τk2​q,s2​q,1.\frac{\tau_{1}}{2q},\ldots,\frac{\tau_{k}}{2q},\frac{s}{2q},1.

The strict inverse-CDF convention gives exactly the rule u<su<s and replay of records at times at most uu. Rounding a time upward changes each boundary by at most 1/(2​q​G)≤1/G1/(2qG)\leq 1/G. There are at most nn boundaries, so a probe changes category with conditional probability at most n/Gn/G. A Poisson count has mean two. Summing over at most nn arrivals and including the collision event bounds this first coupling error by 4​N2/G4N^{2}/G. Before a discrepancy, candidate realizations and basis replays can be coupled identically. The bound holds at every possible history at which the continuation is entered and for every fixed actual vector and order.

Next replace each Poisson count ZZ by its law conditioned on Z≤TZ\leq T. The moment bound

Pr⁡(Z>T)≤𝔼​2Z2T+1=e22T+1<4 2−T\Pr(Z>T)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}2^{Z}}{2^{T+1}}=\frac{e^{2}}{2^{T+1}}<4\,2^{-T}

gives error at most 4​N​2−T≤ρ/24N2^{-T}\leq\rho/2 over the run. Couple counts identically when Z≤TZ\leq T; otherwise generate a fresh conditional count and declare failure. This has the required conditional marginal.

Finally replace all rational categorical draws by the bounded-bit primitive. There are at most CcatC_{\rm cat} draws: each layer uses at most N+2N+2; the at most N⁡(1+T)N(1+T) reference realizations used by the continuation use at most NN coordinate draws each; and the remaining draws comprise at most NN screens, NN counts, and N​TNT prefixes. Every category list has size at most J0J_{0}. Until the first discrepancy, histories and the next categorical laws coincide. A conditional union bound and Lemma 31 give error at most Ccat​J0/GC_{\rm cat}J_{0}/G. Combining the three steps with (C.1) proves total error at most ρ\rho.

On the failed coupling, the ideal algorithm’s possible advantage is at most the realized integral optimum: both algorithms are feasible and have nonnegative reward. The failure bound is uniform conditional on the actual values. Averaging therefore loses at most ρ​F0\rho F_{0}, with no range restriction on those values. ∎

C.3 Running time

Every arithmetic operand has polynomial bit length, every categorical draw uses a fixed number of bits, and each probe count is at most TT. The Poisson integer weights have O⁡(T​log⁡(T+2))O(T\log(T+2)) bits. Thus all loops and all arithmetic work have polynomial worst-case bounds in N,LN,L. For fixed parameters, K,T=O⁡(log⁡(N+2))K,T=O(\log(N+2)), m=O⁡(N​log⁡(N+2))m=O(N\log(N+2)), and ℓbit=O⁡(log⁡(N+2)+log⁡(sin+1))\ell_{\rm bit}=O(\log(N+2)+\log(s_{\rm in}+1)).

The outer policy uses O⁡(N3​log3⁡(N+2))O(N^{3}\log^{3}(N+2)) matroid independence queries. A fresh reference realization requires one greedy basis computation and at most nn exchange replays. The canonical shrinking scan costs O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) queries per replay, so a reference realization costs O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) queries. There is at most one continuation. The bounded-bit count is no larger, in the categorical coupling, than a Poisson count conditioned on being at most TT; its mean is at most two. Thus the continuation algorithm evaluates O⁡(N)O(N) reference realizations in expectation and at most N⁡(1+T)=O⁡(N​log⁡(N+2))N(1+T)=O(N\log(N+2)) reference realizations on every outcome. The resulting total query bounds are

O⁡(N4)in expectation,O⁡(N4​log⁡(N+2))in the worst case.O(N^{4})\quad\text{in expectation},\qquad O(N^{4}\log(N+2))\quad\text{in the worst case}.

In particular, when matroid independence queries themselves take polynomial time, this is a polynomial-time algorithm in the complete rational input model.

Appendix D Certifying the general matroid bound

The algorithm uses the rational parameters

δ=74096,θ=367878301109,η=2475000,s=52,ε=10−6,ρ=ε3,ε0=1.14⋅10−6.\delta=\frac{7}{4096},\quad\theta=\frac{367878301}{10^{9}},\quad\eta=\frac{247}{5000},\quad s=\frac{5}{2},\quad\varepsilon=10^{-6},\quad\rho=\varepsilon^{3},\quad\varepsilon_{0}=1.14\cdot 10^{-6}. (D.1)

Two observations allow a slightly better choice of θ\theta. The threshold step is used only for |q−1|<3​δ|q-1|<3\delta. Also, although the curves a⁡(q)a(q) and 1−e−1/q1-e^{-1/q} are nearly tangent at q=1q=1, their gap decreases quadratically away from that point. Proof of Theorem 1.

First consider explicit finite distributions with rational values and probabilities. Use the parameters in Lemma 33. Proposition 24 gives the ideal policy expected reward at least (1−θ−ρ)​F0(1-\theta-\rho)F_{0}. Lemma 32 loses at most another ρ​F0\rho F_{0}, so the implemented policy obtains (1−θ−2​ρ)​F0>(1−1/e+ε0)​F0(1-\theta-2\rho)F_{0}>(1-1/e+\varepsilon_{0})F_{0} when F0>0F_{0}>0. For F0=0F_{0}=0 the asserted inequality holds trivially. The query bounds and worst-case polynomial arithmetic and random-bit bounds are those of Appendix C.

For general distributions, discard loops and assume F0>0F_{0}>0. Put β=1−θ−2​ρ\beta=1-\theta-2\rho and c=1−1/e+ε0c=1-1/e+\varepsilon_{0}, so β>c\beta>c. For any τ>0\tau>0, truncation and downward rounding to a finite rational grid produce independent Ze≤XeZ_{e}\leq X_{e}, bounded by a rational BB, with 𝔼​OPT⁡(M,Z)≥F0−τ\mathbb{E}\operatorname{OPT}(M,Z)\geq F_{0}-\tau. Indeed, the truncated optima increase to the original optimum, and rounding loses at most NN times the grid width. Approximate each discretized marginal by a positive rational probability vector on the same support. This gives a product distribution YY whose joint total variation distance from ZZ is at most any prescribed γ>0\gamma>0. Here the total variation distance between two distributions PP and QQ on a finite set is 12​∑x|P⁡(x)−Q⁡(x)|\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{x}|P(x)-Q(x)|; equivalently, it is the minimum probability that coupled draws from PP and QQ differ.

Run the finite algorithm designed for YY on the rounded values ZZ. Couple YY and ZZ and use the same arrival order and internal randomness. The two rewards coincide whenever their value vectors coincide, and both rewards and both offline optima lie in [0,N​B][0,NB]. Hence the expected reward on ZZ is at least

β​𝔼​OPT⁡(M,Z)−(1+β)​N​B​γ≥β​F0−β​τ−(1+β)​N​B​γ.\beta\,\mathbb{E}\operatorname{OPT}(M,Z)-(1+\beta)NB\gamma\geq\beta F_{0}-\beta\tau-(1+\beta)NB\gamma.

At an actual arrival, form ZeZ_{e} from XeX_{e} and feed it to this policy. The accepted set earns at least its rounded value. Choose τ\tau and then γ\gamma so that β​τ+(1+β)​N​B​γ<(β−c)​F0\beta\tau+(1+\beta)NB\gamma<(\beta-c)F_{0}. This proves the same factor cc for general distributions. Only the explicit finite rational model is used in the computational claim. ∎
